title: The Pok\'emon Theorem: Fairness Criteria Can't Catch 'Em All
claim: Finite checklists of criteria leave substantial residual unfairness, and approximately fair features obey a derived tradeoff frontier that a linear program attains.
layout: 3 stacked rows of 3 dataset panels, top-to-bottom, shaded impossible region
description: A tall figure made of three stacked rows, each with three small plots, one per dataset. The datasets are Adult, COMPAS and ACS PUMS. Each row has a bold question as its title, followed by a legend. Row A uses log-log curves of the share of MMD² left against the number of criteria m. A blue true-residual curve with a confidence band sits far below a red worst-case curve, and a gray noise-level band runs along the bottom. Row B is scatter plots of signal against unfairness. Blue squares, orange circles and green triangles show fair-feature methods. A red bound line cuts off a pink 'impossible' region at upper left. Row C repeats the scatter plots and adds a blue frontier line, open circles for test rows, and a black point labeled ||ω||_sep. The eye goes first to the red-versus-blue contrast in row A.
caption: (A) True residual unfairness after the best $m$ criteria (blue) and the worst-case residual of [ref] (red). (B) Predictive signal vs.\ unfairness of fair feature methods, one point per setting of their fairness weight. (C) The frontier from the linear program, fit on training and validation rows (line) and measured on test rows (circles). In (B) and (C), the red line is the bound of [ref], and no rule can lie in the shaded region above it. Test-row values are averaged over ten random splits of each dataset, and blue bands are 95% intervals.
abstract: Debates around algorithmic fairness rarely end. Models considered "fair" by one criterion are soon shown to be unfair by another. We prove that this is unavoidable. Satisfying any finite checklist of fairness criteria never certifies fairness itself, since the model may always violate yet another criterion. We call this the PokÃ©mon theorem: you can't catch them all. In fact, trying to catch all criteria recovers the classical impossibility theorems. Since these violations come from differences between the groups' data, a natural remedy would be to make the data fair by learning fair features. Unfortunately, this, too, is impossible: features that scrub out sensitive group information also scrub out all predictive signal. While exact fairness is out of reach, approximate fairness is not. We derive the Pareto frontier between fairness and predictive signal for approximately fair features, and show how to attain it.
